lessons.title: Arrays describe data and shape
lessons.motivation: Shape records what each axis represents, while dtype constrains stored values.
lessons.progression: Read a feature table, then reshape and test an integer conversion.
lessons.terms: ndarray, dtype, shape, ndim, size, reshape, scalar.
lessons.math: Rows are observations; columns are ordered features.
lessons.worked: np.array([[2,10],[1,5],[3,15]]) has shape (3,2), ndim 2 and size 6; reshape(2,3) preserves six elements but changes their row grouping.
lessons.misconception: Number of rows is not ndim; reshaping does not create information or preserve semantic row meaning.

objectives.outcome: Distinguish list behavior from numeric array behavior.
objectives.assessment: Predict list repetition versus elementwise array multiplication.
objectives.remediation: Compare type-tagged traces.

objectives.outcome: Read rows/features and predict shape, ndim and size.
objectives.assessment: Diagnose a feature/observation-axis reversal.
objectives.remediation: Label a small matrix with row IDs and feature names.

objectives.outcome: Check element-count compatibility before reshape.
objectives.assessment: Select a valid and invalid requested shape.
objectives.remediation: Count elements before drawing the new grid.

objectives.outcome: Choose numeric dtype and recognize truncating integer conversion.
objectives.assessment: Predict conversion of supplied decimal values.
objectives.remediation: Inspect original values against the dtype result.

lessons.title: Indexing, masks, views and copies
lessons.motivation: Selection changes axes and may share data with its source.
lessons.progression: Contrast dropped versus retained axes, then edit a view/copy.
lessons.terms: axis, integer index, slice, boolean mask, view, copy.
lessons.math: Selecting a row versus a column changes vector shape and meaning.
lessons.worked: With X=np.array([[2,10],[1,5],[3,15]]), X[:,0] has shape (3,), while X[:,0:1] has shape (3,1). A basic slice may share data; .copy() makes an independent array. The array constructor is required: a plain Python nested list does not support X[:,0].
lessons.misconception: (3,) and (3,1) are not interchangeable; a selected array is not always an independent copy.

objectives.outcome: Predict values and shape after row/column indexing.
objectives.assessment: Choose a changed slice result and explain a dropped axis.
objectives.remediation: Draw retained axes and their lengths.

objectives.outcome: Apply a Boolean mask to matching observations.
objectives.assessment: Select retained rows and paired targets.
objectives.remediation: Compare mask length and selected row IDs.

objectives.outcome: Distinguish shared view edits from explicit copy edits.
objectives.assessment: Repair a supplied accidental source mutation.
objectives.remediation: Trace source and view storage relationships.

objectives.outcome: Explain mask conjunction with parentheses and array operators.
objectives.assessment: Choose a valid bounded (condition)&(condition) expression.
objectives.remediation: Contrast scalar and with elementwise &.

lessons.title: Broadcasting is shape reasoning
lessons.motivation: Broadcasting aligns coordinates; legal arithmetic can still describe the wrong operation.
lessons.progression: Compare per-feature bias, per-row offsets and an incompatible shape.
lessons.terms: trailing axis, singleton dimension, broadcast, compatible/incompatible.
lessons.math: Bias addition; rowwise versus columnwise offsets.
lessons.worked: X shape (3,2) plus b shape (2,) gives (3,2). Adding a (3,) vector fails; reshaping it to (3,1) deliberately creates per-row offsets.
lessons.misconception: Matching total element counts does not establish broadcast compatibility; a legal broadcast may still represent the wrong operation.

objectives.outcome: Align trailing dimensions and apply singleton expansion.
objectives.assessment: Predict compatibility of a new shape pair.
objectives.remediation: Right-align dimensions and mark equality or 1.

objectives.outcome: Select the intended bias orientation rather than merely legal arithmetic.
objectives.assessment: Repair a row/column offset bug and justify the semantic axis.
objectives.remediation: Attach a named meaning to each offset dimension.

objectives.outcome: Predict an outer-style result from (m,1)+(n,).
objectives.assessment: Choose result shape and one worked cell.
objectives.remediation: Expand the small grid of pairwise sums.

objectives.outcome: Recognize an incompatible operation and choose a deliberate repair.
objectives.assessment: Select reject/reshape options without pretending all reshapes preserve meaning.
objectives.remediation: Check both shape legality and data interpretation.

lessons.title: Vectorized predictions replace repeated scalar work
lessons.motivation: Vectorization packages the same ordered weighted predictions for many observations.
lessons.progression: Match scalar contributions to Xw+b, then expose repeated bias or shuffled targets.
lessons.terms: elementwise operation, vectorization, coefficient, bias, prediction, residual.
lessons.math: Xw+b and residual ŷ−y; distinguish multiplication from reduction.
lessons.worked: Define X=np.array([[2,10],[1,5]]) and w=np.array([100,-2]); with b=50, X@w+b gives [230,140]. X*w gives per-feature contributions [[200,-20],[100,-10]], not final predictions. A Python list is not silently treated as an ndarray.
lessons.misconception: Vectorization does not mean every * is a dot product; broadcasting bias in the wrong place can double-count it.

objectives.outcome: Map a scalar loop to elementwise contributions.
objectives.assessment: Predict the contribution table for changed weights.
objectives.remediation: Review dot-product term multiplication before summing.

objectives.outcome: Compute ordered vectorized predictions with bias once per observation.
objectives.assessment: Repair a missing reduction or repeated bias and justify dimensions.
objectives.remediation: Compare each vector result with the scalar row formula.

objectives.outcome: Keep residual sign and feature/target row pairing.
objectives.assessment: Identify swapped targets or y−ŷ versus ŷ−y.
objectives.remediation: Match row IDs and the existing Regression residual convention.

objectives.outcome: Explain equivalence rather than assert universal speed superiority.
objectives.assessment: Choose output equivalence evidence from fixed loops/arrays.
objectives.remediation: Check values/shapes first; do not grade timing.

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication and transposes
lessons.motivation: Matrix multiplication contracts one shared axis rather than multiplying cells independently.
lessons.progression: Expand one output cell, then compare transpose/order and an invalid product.
lessons.terms: matmul, @, transpose, inner dimension, elementwise product.
lessons.worked: np.array([[1,2],[3,4]]) @ np.array([10,1]) gives [12,34]. Elementwise multiplication of those arrays gives [[10,2],[30,4]]. The @ operator here has ndarray operands, not raw nested lists.
lessons.misconception: @ is not *; transpose does not arbitrarily fix feature meaning; multiplication order matters.

objectives.outcome: Check legal dimensions for matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products.
objectives.assessment: Select output shapes or a defined incompatibility.
objectives.remediation: Pair the inner dimensions and keep outer dimensions.

objectives.outcome: Distinguish elementwise multiplication from matrix multiplication.
objectives.assessment: Repair a prediction expression and explain its contraction axis.
objectives.remediation: Expand one row's scalar dot product.

objectives.outcome: Predict a transpose and its feature/observation interpretation.
objectives.assessment: Choose the transposed grid with labels preserved.
objectives.remediation: Swap axis labels rather than just copying numbers.

objectives.outcome: Recognize order-dependent products and reject a meaningless inverse shortcut.
objectives.assessment: Choose valid composition order in a new small matrix trace.
objectives.remediation: Recall transformation composition and numerical solvers.

lessons.title: Reductions, missingness and numeric limits
lessons.motivation: Reduction removes an axis and changes the denominator/units of the summary.
lessons.progression: Compare feature/row means, then ddof and an all-missing column.
lessons.terms: sum, mean, axis, keepdims, variance, ddof, isnan, nanmean, finite.
lessons.math: Sample versus population variance; reduction outputs and units.
lessons.worked: For X=np.array([[1,10],[3,20]]), X.mean(axis=0) gives [2,15] and X.mean(axis=1) gives [5.5,11.5]. np.var([1,3]) is 1 at ddof=0 and 2 at ddof=1.
lessons.misconception: Axis 0 reduces over observations; NaN is not zero; default variance conventions differ across libraries.

objectives.outcome: Predict reduction values and result shape.
objectives.assessment: Choose sum/mean output for a new small matrix.
objectives.remediation: Cross out the reduced axis.

objectives.outcome: Choose the correct axis and denominator for a stated statistic.
objectives.assessment: Repair a per-feature mean/variance claim and explain units/ddof.
objectives.remediation: Count contributing observations and revisit sample/population definitions.

objectives.outcome: Distinguish missing, zero and nonfinite outputs.
objectives.assessment: Choose the correct missingness policy and flag an all-missing column.
objectives.remediation: Compare value masks rather than formatted display.

objectives.outcome: Identify unsafe dtype/finite assumptions without changing old math semantics.
objectives.assessment: Reject a supplied overflow/nonfinite result as a valid model statistic.
objectives.remediation: Inspect dtype bounds and explicit finite checks.

cases.misconception: Both containers repeat their entries because their original values match.

cases.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[3, 10], [4, 5], [5, 15]], dtype=np.int64)
y = np.array([100, 200, 300], dtype=np.int64)
row_ids = ['H1', 'H2', 'H3']
mask = X[:, 0] > 3
result = {'rows': [row_id for row_id, keep in zip(row_ids, mask) if keep], 'X': X[mask], 'y': y[mask]}
cases.reason: Apply the same observation mask to X, y and row IDs. The retained targets belong to H2 and H3, not merely the first two original targets.
cases.misconception: After filtering X, taking the first equally many targets preserves pairing because the lengths agree.

import numpy as np
X = np.array([[3, 10], [4, 5], [5, 15]], dtype=np.int64)
view = X[:, 0]
copy = X[:, 0].copy()
view[0] = 11
result = [X, view, copy]
cases.reason: This basic slice shares source storage; editing its first value changes X. The explicit copy keeps the values from before the edit. Selection is not automatically an independent copy.
cases.misconception: A basic slice is always independent, while copy() links its values back to the original array.
